title: Minimum spanning trees
description:
Undirected weighted graphs are edge lists of `(a, b, cost)`:

```cpp
using CEdges = std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, long long>>;

long long kruskal(int n, CEdges edges, std::vector<std::tuple<int, int, long long>>& chosen);   // -1 if not connected
long long prim(int n, const CEdges& edges);                                                     // -1 if not connected
long long connectPoints(const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& points);                       // Manhattan distances, O(n^2)
std::vector<std::vector<int>> clusters(int n, CEdges edges, int k);
```

- `kruskal` sorts the edges by cost (ties: keep the input order, so use a **stable** sort), adds each one unless union-find says it closes a cycle, fills `chosen` with the edges used in that order, and returns the total. If the graph is not connected, return -1 (and `chosen` holds the spanning forest).
- `prim` grows one tree from vertex 0 with a min-heap; it must give the same total as `kruskal`.
- `connectPoints`: every pair of points can be joined at a cost equal to their Manhattan distance `|x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|`. Return the cheapest total that connects all points, using the heap-free O(n²) Prim from lesson 5.04 (the tests use 3,000 points: 4.5 million possible edges).
- `clusters`: run Kruskal but stop when there are `k` components left. Return the components, each sorted, and the list sorted by first element.
hints: In the O(n²) Prim, keep `best[v]`, the cheapest known cost of attaching point `v` to the tree. Each step picks the outside point with the smallest `best`, adds it, and lowers `best` for every other outside point using the distance to the new tree point.
For clusters, Kruskal reaches `k` components exactly when it has made `n - k` successful unions; stop there and group the vertices by their union-find root.
